danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 3
paragraphs: I 1811 boede der i Moskva en fransk læge — Métivier — der hurtigt var kommet på mode. Han var overordentlig høj, flot, elskværdig som franskmænd er, og var, som hele Moskva sagde, en usædvanlig dygtig læge. Han blev modtaget i de bedste huse ikke blot som læge, men som ligemand.

Fyrst Nikolaj havde altid gjort nar af lægekunsten, men havde i den senere tid på mademoiselle Bouriennes anbefaling tilladt denne læge at besøge ham og var blevet vant til ham. Métivier kom til fyrsten cirka to gange om ugen.

Den sjette december — Skt. Nikolaj-dagen og fyrstens navnedag — kom hele Moskva til fyrstens hoveddør, men han gav ordre til ikke at lukke nogen ind og kun invitere et lille antal til middag efter en liste, han gav til fyrstinde Marja.

Métivier, der kom om morgenen med sine lykønskninger, anså det for passende i sin egenskab af læge de forcer la consigne,* som han sagde til fyrstinde Marja, og gik ind for at se fyrsten. Det tilfældigt sig, at fyrsten den morgen på sin navnedag var i et af sine værste humører. Han havde gået rundt i huset hele morgenen og fundet fejl ved alle og ladet som om han ikke forstod, hvad der blev sagt til ham, og som om han ikke selv blev forstået. Fyrstinde Marja kendte godt dette humør af stille, grublende pirrelighed, som normalt kulminerede i et vredesudbrud, og hun gik den morgen omkring som stod hun foran en spændt og ladt pistol og ventede den uundgåelige eksplosion. Indtil lægens ankomst var morgenen gået sikkert. Efter at have lukket lægen ind satte fyrstinde Marja sig med en bog i salonen nær døren, hvorfra hun kunne høre alt, hvad der foregik i arbejdsværelset.
* At forcere vagten.

Først hørte hun kun Métiviers stemme, så sin fars, så begyndte begge stemmer at tale på samme tid, døren blev revet op, og på tærsklen stod Métiviers smukke skikkelse med sit sorte hår i uorden og fyrsten i morgenkappe og kalot, med ansigtet forvrænget af raseri og pupillerne rullet nedad.
»Forstår De det ikke?« skreg fyrsten, »men det gør jeg! Fransk spion, Buonapartes slave, spion, ud af mit hus! Forsvind, siger jeg!...« og han smækkede døren i.
Métivier trak på skuldrene og gik hen til mademoiselle Bourienne, der ved lyden af skrigene var kommet løbende ind fra et tilstødende værelse.
»Fyrsten er ikke helt rask: galde og blodtilstrømning til hovedet. Bevar roen, jeg kommer igen i morgen,« sagde Métivier; og idet han førte fingrene til læberne, skyndte han sig bort.
Gennem arbejdsværelsets dør lød lyden af tøffelklædte fødder og råbet: »Spioner, forrædere, forrædere overalt! Ikke et øjebliks fred i mit eget hus!«

Efter Métiviers afrejse kaldte den gamle fyrste sin datter ind, og hans vredes fulde tyngde faldt over hende. Hun var skyld i, at en spion var blevet lukket ind. Havde han ikke sagt hende — jo, sagt hende — at hun skulle lave en liste og ikke lukke nogen ind, der ikke stod på listen? Hvorfor var den slyngel så blevet lukket ind? Hun var årsag til det hele. Med hende, sagde han, kunne han ikke have et øjebliks fred og heller ikke dø i ro.

»Nej, frue! Vi må skilles, vi må skilles! Forstå det, forstå det! Jeg kan ikke udholde mere,« sagde han og forlod stuen. Så, som bange for at hun kunne finde et eller andet middel til trøst, vendte han tilbage og forsøgte at virke rolig og tilføjede: »Og tro ikke, jeg har sagt det i et øjeblik af vrede. Jeg er rolig. Jeg har tænkt over det, og det bliver gennemført — vi må skilles; så find dig et sted at bo...« Men han kunne ikke beherske sig og skreg med den voldsomhed, som kun den, der elsker, er i stand til, og tydeligvis lidende selv, rystede han næverne ad hende og skreg:
»Bare en eller anden fjols ville gifte sig med hende!« Så slog han døren i, sendte bud efter mademoiselle Bourienne og faldt til ro i sit arbejdsværelse.
Klokken to samledes de seks udvalgte gæster til middag.

Disse gæster — den berømte grev Rostoptjin, fyrst Lopukhin med sin nevø, general Tsjatrof, en gammel krigskammerat af fyrsten, og af den yngre generation Pierre og Boris Drubetskoj — ventede på fyrsten i salonen.

Boris, der var kommet til Moskva på orlov et par dage forinden, havde været ivrig efter at blive præsenteret for fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskij og havde formået at indynde sig så godt, at den gamle fyrste i hans tilfælde gjorde en undtagelse fra reglen om ikke at modtage ungkarle i sit hus.

Fyrstens hus hørte ikke til det, man kalder det fashionable selskab, men hans lille kreds — selvom der ikke blev talt meget om den i byen — var en kreds, det var mere smigrende at blive modtaget i end nogen anden. Boris havde indset dette ugen forinden, da øverstbefalende i hans nærværelse inviterede Rostoptjin til middag på Skt. Nikolaj-dagen, og Rostoptjin havde svaret, at han ikke kunne komme:
»Den dag aflægger jeg altid mine andagtsbesøg ved fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskijs relikvier.«
»Åh ja, ja!« svarede den øverstbefalende. »Hvordan har han det?...«

Den lille gruppe, der samledes før middagen i den højtloftede, gammeldags salon med dens gamle møbler, lignede et retsmødes højtidelige forsamling. Alle var tavse eller talte dæmpet. Fyrst Nikolaj kom ind, alvorlig og tavs. Fyrstinde Marja virkede endnu mere stille og sky end sædvanligt. Gæsterne var tilbageholdende med at henvende sig til hende, idet de følte, at hun ikke var i stemning til deres samtale. Grev Rostoptjin alene holdt samtalen i gang, snart med de seneste bynyheder, snart med den seneste politiske sladder.

Lopukhin og den gamle general deltog af og til i samtalen. Fyrst Bolkonskij lyttede som en dommer, der modtager en rapport, og kun nu og da, tavst eller med et kort ord, viste, at han tog til efterretning, hvad der blev berettet. Tonen i samtalen var af en art, der tydede på, at ingen billigede, hvad der skete i den politiske verden. Begivenheder blev fortalt, der tydeligt bekræftede den opfattelse, at alt gik fra ondt til værre, men hvad enten taleren fortalte en historie eller gav sin mening til kende, standsede han altid, eller blev standset, på det punkt, ud over hvilket hans kritik kunne berøre kejseren selv.

Ved middagen faldt talen på de seneste politiske nyheder: Napoleons beslaglæggelse af hertugen af Oldenburgs territorium og den russiske note, fjendtlig mod Napoleon, der var sendt til alle de europæiske hoffer.

»Bonaparte behandler Europa som en sørøver behandler et erobret skib,« sagde grev Rostoptjin og gentog en sætning, han havde brugt flere gange før. »Man undrer sig kun over de kronede hoveders langmodighed eller blindhed. Nu er Pavens tur kommet, og Bonaparte viger ikke tilbage for at afsætte den katolske kirkes overhoved — og alligevel tier alle! Vores kejser alene har protesteret mod beslaglæggelsen af hertugen af Oldenburgs territorium, og endda...« Grev Rostoptjin standsede, da han mærkede, at han havde nået den grænse, ud over hvilken kritik var umulig.

»Andre territorier er blevet tilbudt til gengæld for hertugdømmet Oldenburg,« sagde fyrst Bolkonskij. »Han flytter rundt på hertugerne, som jeg kunne flytte mine livegne fra Lysehøje til Bogutsjarovo eller mine rjazanske godser.«
»Hertugen af Oldenburg bærer sine ulykker med beundringsværdig karakterstyrke og resignation,« bemærkede Boris, idet han respektfuldt blandede sig.

Han sagde dette, fordi han på sin rejse fra Petersborg havde haft den ære at blive præsenteret for hertugen. Fyrst Bolkonskij kastede et blik på den unge mand, som om han ville sige noget til svar, men ombestemte sig, da han tydeligvis anså ham for for ung.

»Jeg har læst vores protest vedrørende Oldenburg-affæren og var overrasket over, hvor dårligt noten var formuleret,« bemærkede grev Rostoptjin i den afslappede tone hos en mand, der beskæftiger sig med et emne, han kender til bunds.
Pierre kiggede på Rostoptjin med naiv forbavselse, uforstående over for hvorfor han skulle være generet af notens dårlige sammensætning.
»Gør det noget, greve, hvordan noten er formuleret,« spurgte han, »så længe dens indhold er kraftfuldt?«
»Min kære ven, med vores fem hundrede tusind soldater burde det være let at have en god stil,« svarede grev Rostoptjin.
Pierre forstod nu grevens utilfredshed med notens formulering.

»Man skulle tro, der var skriverkarle nok,« bemærkede den gamle fyrste. »Der i Petersborg skriver de altid — ikke kun noter, men endda nye love. Min Andrej dér har skrevet et helt bind love for Rusland. I vore dage skriver de altid!« og han lo unaturligt.
Der var en kortvarig pause i samtalen; den gamle general rensede struben for at tiltrække opmærksomhed.
»Har De hørt om den seneste begivenhed ved paraden i Petersborg? Den figur, den nye franske ambassadør skar.«
»Nå? Ja, jeg hørte noget; han sagde noget klodset i Hans Majestæts nærværelse.«

»Hans Majestæt henledte opmærksomheden på Grenaderdivisionen og på forbi-marschen,« fortsatte generalen, »og det synes, at ambassadøren ikke tog notits og tillod sig at svare: 'I Frankrig lægger vi ikke vægt på den slags småting!' Kejseren nedlod sig ikke til at svare. Ved den næste parade, siger de, nedlod kejseren sig ikke en eneste gang til at tiltale ham.«
Alle tav. Om denne kendsgerning, der angik kejseren personligt, var det umuligt at fælde nogen dom.

»Uforskammede fyrer!« sagde fyrsten. »Kender De Métivier? Jeg smed ham ud af mit hus i morges. Han var her; de lukkede ham ind trods min anmodning om, at de ikke skulle lukke nogen ind,« sagde han og kiggede vredt på sin datter.

Og han fortalte hele sin samtale med den franske læge og de grunde, der overbeviste ham om, at Métivier var en spion. Selvom disse grunde var meget utilstrækkelige og uklare, fremkom der ingen indvendinger.
Efter stegen blev der serveret champagne. Gæsterne rejste sig for at lykønske den gamle fyrste. Fyrstinde Marja gik også hen til ham.

Han gav hende et koldt, vredt blik og rakte hende sin rynkede, glatbarberede kind at kysse. Hele hans ansigtsudtryk fortalte hende, at han ikke havde glemt morgenens samtale, at hans beslutning stod fast, og at kun gæsternes tilstedeværelse forhindrede ham i at tale om det nu.
Da de gik ind i salonen, hvor der blev serveret kaffe, satte de gamle mænd sig sammen.
Fyrst Nikolaj blev mere livlig og gav udtryk for sine synspunkter om den forestående krig.

Han sagde, at vores krige mod Bonaparte ville være katastrofale, så længe vi søgte alliancer med tyskerne og stak os ind i europæiske anliggender, som vi var blevet trukket ind i af Tilsit-freden. »Vi bør hverken kæmpe for eller mod Østrig. Vores politiske interesser ligger alle i øst, og hvad Bonaparte angår, er det eneste at have en bevæbnet grænse og en fast politik, og han vil aldrig vove at krydse den russiske grænse, som tilfældet var i 1807!«

»Hvordan kan vi kæmpe mod franskmændene, fyrste?« sagde grev Rostoptjin. »Kan vi bevæbne os mod vore lærere og guder? Se på vore unge mænd, se på vore damer! Franskmændene er vore guder: Paris er vort Himmerig.«
Han begyndte at tale højere, tydeligvis for at blive hørt af alle.

»Franske kjoler, franske idéer, franske følelser! Nu har De jaget Métivier ud i nakkeskindet, fordi han er franskmand og en slyngel, men vore damer kravler efter ham på knæ. Jeg var til selskab i går aftes, og dér var tre af fem damer romersk-katolske med pavens aflad til at brodere om søndagen. Og de selv sidder der næsten nøgne, som skiltene på vores offentlige bade, om De tilgiver mig. Ak, når man ser på vore unge mennesker, fyrste, kunne man have lyst til at tage Peter den Stores gamle knippel ud af museet og prygle dem på russisk vis, til alt vrøvlet springer ud af dem.«
Alle tav. Den gamle fyrste kiggede på Rostoptjin med et smil og nikkede bifaldende.
»Nå, farvel, Deres Excellence, bevar Dem vel!« sagde Rostoptjin, idet han med sin karakteristiske kvikhed rejste sig og rakte hånden ud til fyrsten.
»Farvel, min kære ven... Hans ord er musik, jeg bliver aldrig træt af at høre ham!« sagde den gamle fyrste, idet han holdt fast i hånden og rakte sin kind frem til et kys.
I Rostoptjins fodspor rejste de øvrige sig også.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: In 1811 there lived in Moscow a French doctor named Metivier who had rapidly become fashionable. He was enormously tall, handsome, charming in the French manner, and was, as all Moscow said, an extraordinarily clever physician. He was received in the best houses not merely as a doctor but as an equal.

Prince Nicholas had always ridiculed medicine, but lately, on Mademoiselle Bourienne's advice, he had allowed this doctor to visit him and had grown accustomed to him. Metivier came to see the prince about twice a week.

On December 6th — St. Nicholas's Day and the prince's name day — all Moscow came to the prince's door, but he gave orders to admit no one and to invite to dinner only a small number of guests whose names he gave Princess Mary.

Metivier, who came that morning with his congratulations, considered it proper in his capacity as doctor to force his way past the barrier, as he explained to Princess Mary, and went in to see the prince. It happened that on this name-day morning the prince was in one of his worst moods. He had been going around the house since dawn finding fault with everyone and pretending not to understand what was said to him and not to be understood himself. Princess Mary knew this mood of quiet, absorbed grouchiness well — it generally built to an explosion of rage — and she went about all morning as though walking past a loaded gun, waiting for the inevitable shot. Until the doctor's arrival the morning had passed safely. After admitting the doctor, Princess Mary sat in the drawing room with a book near the door through which she could hear everything from the study.
* To force the barrier.

At first she heard only Metivier's voice, then her father's, then both speaking at once. The door was flung open and on the threshold appeared the handsome figure of the terrified Metivier with his shock of black hair — and behind him the prince in his dressing gown and fez, his face contorted with fury and the pupils of his eyes rolled down.
"You don't understand?" the prince shouted. "But I do! French spy, Bonaparte's lackey — spy — get out of my house! Out, I tell you!" And he slammed the door.
Metivier shrugged his shoulders and went up to Mademoiselle Bourienne, who had rushed in from the next room at the sound of shouting.
"The prince is not feeling well: a bilious attack and a rush of blood to the head. Don't worry, I'll call again tomorrow," said Metivier; and putting his fingers to his lips, he hurried away.
Through the study door came the sound of shuffling slippers and the cry: "Spies, traitors, traitors everywhere! Not a moment's peace in my own house!"

After Metivier left, the old prince called his daughter in, and the full weight of his fury fell on her. She was to blame for letting a spy in. Hadn't he told her — yes, told her — to make a list, and not admit anyone who wasn't on it? Then why was that scoundrel allowed in? She was the cause of it all. With her, he said, he couldn't have a moment's peace and couldn't die in peace.

"No, madam! We must part — we must part! I want you to understand that — I cannot endure this any longer," he said, and left the room. Then, as if afraid she might find some means of consolation, he came back and — trying to appear calm — added: "And don't think I said this in a fit of temper. I am calm. I've thought it over, and this will be carried out: we must part. Find yourself somewhere to live..." But he couldn't hold himself back, and with the fury that only someone who loves is capable of — clearly suffering himself — he shook his fists at her and screamed:
"If only some fool would marry her!" Then he slammed the door, sent for Mademoiselle Bourienne, and shut himself up in his study.
At two o'clock the six chosen guests assembled for dinner.

These guests — the famous Count Rostopchin, Prince Lopukhin with his nephew, General Chatrov (an old war comrade of the prince's), and from the younger generation Pierre and Boris Drubetskoy — waited for the prince in the drawing room.

Boris, who had come to Moscow on leave a few days earlier, had been eager to be presented to Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky and had managed to ingratiate himself so well that the old prince made an exception to his rule of not receiving bachelors.

The prince's house did not belong to fashionable society, but his small circle — though not much talked about in town — was more flattering to be received in than any other. Boris had realized this the week before, when the commander-in-chief invited Rostopchin to dinner on St. Nicholas's Day in his presence, and Rostopchin had replied that he couldn't come:
"On that day I always go to pay my respects to the relics of Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky."
"Oh, yes, yes!" the commander-in-chief had replied. "How is he?..."

The small group that gathered before dinner in the lofty, old-fashioned drawing room with its antique furniture resembled the solemn assembly of a court of law. Everyone was silent or spoke in low tones. Prince Nicholas entered looking serious and taciturn. Princess Mary seemed even quieter and more reserved than usual. The guests were reluctant to address her, sensing she was in no mood for conversation. Count Rostopchin alone kept the talk alive, sharing the latest town news and political gossip.

Lopukhin and the old general occasionally joined in. Prince Bolkonsky listened like a presiding judge receiving reports, now and then silently or with a brief word indicating that he was taking note. The tone of the conversation made clear that no one approved of what was happening in the political world. Stories were told that obviously confirmed the view that everything was going from bad to worse — but each speaker stopped, or was stopped, at the point where criticism might touch the sovereign himself.
At dinner the conversation turned to the latest political news: Napoleon's seizure of the Duke of Oldenburg's territories and the hostile Russian Note sent to all European courts.

"Bonaparte treats Europe like a pirate treats a captured ship," said Count Rostopchin, repeating a phrase he had used many times. "One can only marvel at the patience — or the blindness — of the crowned heads. Now it's the Pope's turn, and Bonaparte doesn't scruple to depose the head of the Catholic Church — yet everyone keeps silent! Our sovereign alone has protested against the seizure of the Duke of Oldenburg's territory, and even..." Rostopchin paused, feeling he had reached the boundary beyond which criticism was not permitted.

"Other territories have been offered in exchange for the Duchy of Oldenburg," said Prince Bolkonsky. "He shuffles dukes around the way I might move my serfs from Bald Hills to Bogucharovo or my Ryazan estates."
"The Duke of Oldenburg bears his misfortune with admirable strength and dignity," Boris remarked, joining in respectfully.

He said this because on his trip from Petersburg he had had the honor of being presented to the Duke. Prince Bolkonsky glanced at the young man as if about to say something, but changed his mind — evidently considering him too young.
"I've read our protest about the Oldenburg affair and was surprised at how poorly the Note was worded," said Count Rostopchin, in the casual tone of a man speaking on a familiar subject.
Pierre looked at Rostopchin with naive surprise, not understanding why the wording of the Note should bother him.
"Does it matter, Count, how the Note is worded," he asked, "as long as its substance is forceful?"
"My dear fellow, with five hundred thousand troops it should be easy to have good style," replied Count Rostopchin.
Pierre now understood the count's dissatisfaction with the wording of the Note.

"One would have thought there were enough pen-pushers around," remarked the old prince. "Over there in Petersburg they're always scribbling — not just notes but new laws too. My Andrew has written a whole volume of laws for Russia. Everything is writing nowadays!" And he laughed his unnatural laugh.
There was a momentary pause; the old general cleared his throat to draw attention.
"Did you hear about the latest incident at the review in Petersburg? The impression made by the new French ambassador."
"Oh? Yes, I heard something: he said something awkward in His Majesty's presence."

"His Majesty directed attention to the Grenadier division and the march past," the general continued, "and it seems the ambassador paid no attention and took the liberty of replying: 'We in France pay no attention to such trifles!' The Emperor did not condescend to reply. At the next review, they say, the Emperor did not once deign to address him."
All were silent. On this point, which concerned the Emperor personally, no judgment could be passed.

"Impudent scoundrels!" said the prince. "You know Metivier? I threw him out of my house this morning. He was here — they let him in despite my orders that no one was to be admitted," he said, glancing angrily at his daughter.
And he told the whole story of his conversation with the French doctor and the reasons that convinced him Metivier was a spy. Though the reasons were flimsy and unclear, no one raised an objection.
After the roast, champagne was served. The guests rose to congratulate the old prince. Princess Mary also went up to him.

He gave her a cold, angry look and offered her his wrinkled, clean-shaven cheek to kiss. His whole expression told her he had not forgotten the morning's conversation, that his decision stood, and only the presence of guests kept him from saying so now.
When they moved to the drawing room for coffee, the older men sat together.
Prince Nicholas grew more animated and shared his views on the coming war.

He said that our wars with Bonaparte would be disastrous as long as we sought alliances with the Germans and meddled in European affairs, into which we had been dragged by the Treaty of Tilsit. "We ought not to fight either for or against Austria. Our political interests all lie in the East, and as for Bonaparte — all that's needed is an armed frontier and a firm policy, and he will never dare cross the Russian border, as he proved in 1807!"

"How can we fight the French, Prince?" said Count Rostopchin. "Can we take up arms against our teachers and our gods? Look at our young people, look at our ladies! The French are our gods: Paris is our Kingdom of Heaven."
He began speaking louder, clearly intending to be heard by everyone.

"French fashions, French ideas, French feelings! There — you threw Metivier out by the scruff of his neck because he's a Frenchman and a scoundrel, but our ladies crawl after him on their knees. I went to a party last night, and out of five women three were Catholics with papal dispensation to do needlework on Sundays. And they themselves sit around practically naked, like the signboards at our public bathhouses, if you'll pardon the comparison. Ah, when one looks at our young people, Prince, one would like to dig out Peter the Great's old cudgel from the museum and thrash them in the good old Russian way until all the nonsense is beaten out of them."
Everyone was silent. The old prince looked at Rostopchin with a smile and nodded approvingly.
"Well, goodbye, your excellency — keep well!" said Rostopchin, getting up with his characteristic briskness and holding out his hand to the prince.
"Goodbye, my dear fellow... His words are music — I never tire of hearing them!" said the old prince, keeping hold of his hand and offering his cheek to be kissed.
Following Rostopchin's example, the other guests also rose.
